# Beyond Binary Verifiable Rewards: Behavioral Self-Rewarding for SWE Agents

Yiran Wu ^(†)^(†)thanks: Work partially done during an internship at
Microsoft Research. Affiliation: Pennsylvania State University
Email: [yiran.wu@psu.edu](mailto:)    Andrew Zhao
Email: [andrewzhao112@gmail.com](mailto:)    Yurui Chang
Affiliation: Pennsylvania State University
Email: [yuruic@psu.edu](mailto:)    Qingyun Wu Affiliation: AG2AI
Email: [qingyun@ag2.ai](mailto:)    Xuan Feng Affiliation: Microsoft
Research Email: [xuafeng@microsoft.com](mailto:)

###### Abstract

Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) provides reliable
supervision for software engineering agents through executable tests,
but binary rewards fail to distinguish trajectories with substantially
different debugging quality. We investigate whether the current policy
can judge its own trajectories and use these judgments to improve task
performance without a separately trained reward model. To this end, we
introduce Behavioral Self-Rewarding (BSR), a reward-refinement method
that reuses the policy to compare observable debugging behavior among
trajectories from the same task with the same verifier outcome. BSR
aggregates pairwise preferences into task-local scores and converts them
into bounded auxiliary rewards, introducing reward contrast while
preserving the verifier-defined pass/fail ordering. This provides
additional supervision from already-collected trajectories without
requiring new environment interactions. Experiments on SWE-bench
Verified and SWE-bench-Live show consistent improvements across the
evaluated Qwen3-14B and Qwen3-32B configurations, supporting using the
policy’s own comparative judgments as a complementary learning signal
for training software engineering agents.

## 1 Introduction

Large language models are increasingly being deployed as software
engineering (SWE) agents: systems that operate inside real repositories
and produce patches for concrete issues through interaction with
developer tools. Such repository-level software engineering requires an
agent to reason under partial information while interacting with a
changing repository and deciding how to proceed from the observations it
gathers ([Yang et al., 2024](#bib.bib20)). This makes software
engineering both practically important and technically demanding for
language agents, while producing rich multi-step trajectories that
capture how an agent approaches a problem. Recent benchmarks and systems
have made this setting concrete by evaluating agents on real
issue-resolution tasks with executable feedback ([Jimenez et al.,
2024](#bib.bib22); [Xia et al., 2024](#bib.bib31); [Wang et al.,
2025a](#bib.bib35)).

This setting is also a natural fit for reinforcement learning with
verifiable rewards (RLVR), where rewards come from automatic checkers
rather than learned preference models ([Shao et al., 2024](#bib.bib16);
[Guo et al., 2025](#bib.bib17)). Recent work extends RLVR from
single-turn reasoning to multi-step agentic RL, where models learn from
trajectories of actions and observations rather than isolated final
answers ([Chen et al., 2025a](#bib.bib34); [Wang et al.,
2025b](#bib.bib38); [Luo et al., 2025](#bib.bib39)). Software
engineering is a compelling instance because interactions are
long-horizon and behaviorally complex, while final patches can often be
validated through repository test suites ([Pan et al.,
2024](#bib.bib32); [Wei et al., 2026](#bib.bib19); [Jain et al.,
2025](#bib.bib33); [Golubev et al., 2025](#bib.bib36)).

However, binary test outcomes compress rich interaction trajectories
into a single success or failure signal. Failed trajectories can vary
substantially in debugging quality: some locate relevant code, gather
useful evidence, or make progress toward a fix, while others achieve
little, yet both receive reward zero. Under group-relative objectives
such as GRPO or leave-one-out PPO, rollout groups with identical
verifier outcomes have zero reward variance and therefore zero
outcome-derived relative advantages ([Shao et al., 2024](#bib.bib16);
[Chen et al., 2025a](#bib.bib34)). Useful distinctions among
already-collected trajectories consequently remain unavailable to the
reward signal. This is particularly costly for SWE agents, whose
rollouts require repeated model inference and tool execution. Several
recent approaches enrich verifier supervision with dense reward-model
scores and learned trajectory evaluations ([Tao et al.,
2026](#bib.bib4); [Han et al., 2026](#bib.bib3); [Shum et al.,
2026](#bib.bib13)). These approaches demonstrate the value of
supervision beyond binary outcomes, but obtain the additional signal
from a separate reward model. Rather than developing another trajectory
scorer, we investigate a complementary question: _can the current policy
itself judge its own SWE trajectories, and how can those judgments be
used to improve its task performance?_

Self-rewarding and LLM-as-a-judge methods motivate this question by
showing that language models can provide evaluative signals for
generated responses and individual reasoning steps ([Yuan et al.,
2024](#bib.bib24); [Zheng et al., 2023](#bib.bib23); [Liu et al.,
2023](#bib.bib40); [Zhang et al., 2025](#bib.bib6)). For interactive SWE
agents, the object of judgment is instead a long-horizon trajectory of
search, inspection, editing, and verification. These trajectories record
not only the final patch but also the evidence gathered, the actions
taken in response, and the checks performed along the way. The challenge
is to turn judgments about this interaction experience into useful
training signals while retaining the distinction between passing and
failing attempts. We therefore study a restricted judging role: the
executable verifier determines the outcome of each attempt, while the
current policy compares attempts at the same task that share that
outcome. This asks the policy for local preferences, rather than an
independent correctness decision or a globally calibrated
trajectory-quality score.

To investigate this question, we introduce _Behavioral Self-Rewarding_
(BSR), a reward-refinement method for multi-step agentic RLVR. For each
software-engineering task, the policy samples multiple trajectories and
receives the ordinary test-based reward. BSR partitions these
trajectories into task-local verifier-outcome buckets and reuses the
current policy to perform pairwise comparisons within each bucket. The
comparisons follow a rubric focused on observable debugging actions and
their outcomes rather than writing style or confidence. Each judgment
identifies a preferred trajectory and a coarse preference-strength
label, which are aggregated into task-local ranking scores. These scores
are normalized and transformed into centered, bounded auxiliary rewards
that supplement the verifier reward. The reward bounds ensure that every
verifier-passing trajectory retains a higher reward than every
verifier-failing trajectory. BSR thus combines current-policy trajectory
comparison with verifier-conditioned reward refinement, using the
policy’s preferences directly in on-policy RL without fitting a separate
trajectory reward model.

BSR integrates with group-relative RL by introducing reward contrast
where binary verification provides none. In all-fail rollout groups,
nonconstant auxiliary rewards can restore group-relative learning
signal; in mixed-outcome groups, they provide finer distinctions among
trajectories sharing an outcome. Reward refinement requires additional
model inference but no new environment interactions. We evaluate BSR
against verifier-only RL to test whether this self-judgment procedure
improves the acting policy. Experiments cover Qwen3-14B and Qwen3-32B on
SWE-bench Verified, SWE-bench-Live Lite, and Terminal-Bench 2.1. BSR
improves average accuracy across the evaluated configurations on all
three benchmarks, with consistent gains in Pass@3 on the two SWE
benchmarks. Ablations examine the reward mapping and the choice of
refined outcome buckets; failure-only refinement achieves the highest
average accuracy and Pass@3 among the tested bucket configurations. In
the random-reward control, using the same auxiliary reward amplitude
range without trajectory rankings does not reproduce these gains.
Together, these results support using the current policy’s comparative
judgments as an additional source of supervision for learning from
repository-level interaction experience.

Figure 1: Overview of Behavioral Self-Rewarding (BSR). Binary rewards
provide no contrast when trajectories share the same verifier outcome,
while BSR ranks them within the outcome group to recover a bounded
learning signal.

## 2 Preliminaries

We consider software-engineering tasks under RLVR: A task $`x`$ consists
of an initial repository state, an issue description, and an executable
verifier. A policy $`\pi_{\theta}`$ interacts with the repository
through developer tools to gather evidence, modify code, and produce a
final patch. For each task, we sample $`K\geq 2`$ trajectories,

|     |     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|     |

       ``` math
       \{\tau_{i}\}_{i=1}^{K}\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x),
       ```                                                   |     | (1) |

where $`\tau_{i}`$ records the full multi-step interaction with the
environment. The verifier assigns a binary reward,

|     |     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|     |

````math
R_{\mathrm{ver}}(\tau_{i})=\begin{cases}1,&\text{if the final patch passes the verifier,}\\
0,&\text{otherwise.}\end{cases}
``` |  | (2) |

In verifier-only RL, the training reward is
$`R_{i}=R_{\mathrm{ver}}(\tau_{i})`$.

Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) computes advantages by
normalizing rewards within each sampled group ([Shao et al.,
2024](#bib.bib16)):

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
A_{i}^{\mathrm{GRPO}}=\frac{R_{i}-\mu_{R}}{\sigma_{R}+\epsilon},\qquad\mu_{R}=\frac{1}{K}\sum_{j=1}^{K}R_{j},\qquad\sigma_{R}=\sqrt{\frac{1}{K}\sum_{j=1}^{K}(R_{j}-\mu_{R})^{2}},
``` |  | (3) |

where $`\epsilon>0`$ ensures numerical stability. LOOP adapts
group-relative optimization to long-horizon interactive agents using a
leave-one-out baseline ([Chen et al., 2025a](#bib.bib34)):

|     |                                                              |     |     |
|-----|--------------------------------------------------------------|-----|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       A_{i}^{\mathrm{LOO}}=R_{i}-\frac{1}{K-1}\sum_{j\neq i}R_{j}.
       ```                                                           |     | (4) |

Both methods use these advantages in clipped policy-gradient objectives
without a learned value model. With binary verifier rewards, all-fail
and all-pass rollout groups have identical rewards and therefore zero
advantages under both formulations. Such groups provide no
reward-derived policy-gradient signal, even when their trajectories
differ substantially in debugging quality. This motivates refining
rewards among trajectories with the same verifier outcome while
retaining verifier-defined task success.

## 3 Method

We introduce *Behavioral Self-Rewarding* (BSR) to study whether the
current policy’s judgments can provide useful supervision for its own
software-engineering training. For each task, we first collect policy
trajectories and their executable verifier outcomes, then reuse the same
model as a post-rollout judge to compare attempts with the same outcome.
The judge receives the task, shared verifier outcome, compact trajectory
representations, and the training task’s reference patch $`p^{\star}`$.
This deliberately asymmetric setup gives the post-rollout judge a
solution reference for interpreting the relevance of observed actions
and edits, while the acting policy generates trajectories without access
to $`p^{\star}`$ during both training and evaluation. The reference is
intended to reduce ambiguity in task-local comparisons; it is provided
as context for the behavioral rubric rather than used to compute an
explicit patch-similarity reward. The resulting preferences are
converted into auxiliary rewards for policy optimization without
training a separate reward model. The refined training reward is

|     |                                         |     |     |
|-----|-----------------------------------------|-----|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       R_{i}=R_{\mathrm{ver}}(\tau_{i})+r_{i},
       ```                                      |     | (5) |

where $`r_{i}`$ is a bounded auxiliary reward derived from the policy’s
within-outcome comparisons. We instantiate this judgment through
pairwise ranking, asking the model to express local preferences rather
than assign absolute trajectory-quality scores. Each comparison concerns
attempts at the same task and can be inspected directly, without
requiring a quality scale calibrated across tasks. Alternative
instantiations based on joint group rankings and absolute rubric scores
are discussed in
Appendix [A.4](#A1.SS4 "A.4 Other Potential Instantiations of Behavioral Reward ‣ Appendix A Additional Method Details ‣ Beyond Binary Verifiable Rewards: Behavioral Self-Rewarding for SWE Agents").

### 3.1 Pairwise Behavioral Ranking

BSR refines the rewards used by group-relative RL. For each task $`x`$,
the current policy samples $`K`$ trajectories, and the verifier assigns
each trajectory a binary outcome:

|     |                                             |     |     |
|-----|---------------------------------------------|-----|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       y_{i}=R_{\mathrm{ver}}(\tau_{i})\in\{0,1\}.
       ```                                          |     | (6) |

We partition the trajectories into task-local verifier-outcome buckets,

|     |                                                          |     |     |
|-----|----------------------------------------------------------|-----|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       B_{y}=\{i\in\{1,\ldots,K\}:y_{i}=y\},\qquad y\in\{0,1\}.
       ```                                                       |     | (7) |

Each outcome bucket has a reward amplitude $`a_{y}\geq 0`$, with
$`a_{y}=0`$ disabling refinement for that outcome. The judge compares
only trajectories from the same task and verifier-outcome bucket. A
failure bucket may contain all $`K`$ trajectories from an all-fail
rollout group or only the failed subset of a mixed-outcome group;
success buckets are handled analogously. This restricts the policy’s
judging role to expressing preferences among attempts with a shared
outcome. The distinction between passing and failing attempts is
preserved by the reward-amplitude constraint in
Equation [15](#S3.E15 "In 3.2 From Pairwise Comparisons to Rewards ‣ 3 Method ‣ Beyond Binary Verifiable Rewards: Behavioral Self-Rewarding for SWE Agents").

1: Task $`x`$, reference patch $`p^{\star}`$, policy $`\pi_{\theta}`$,
group size $`K`$, verifier $`V`$

2: Amplitudes $`a_{y}\geq 0`$ satisfying $`a_{0}+a_{1}<1`$, deadzone
thresholds $`\delta_{y}\geq 0`$, softness parameters $`\tau_{y}>0`$ for
$`y\in\{0,1\}`$

3: Sample trajectories
$`\{\tau_{i}\}_{i=1}^{K}\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x)`$

4: for $`i=1,\ldots,K`$ do

5:   $`y_{i}\leftarrow V(\tau_{i})`$ $`\triangleright`$ $`y_{i}=1`$ if
the trajectory passes the verifier; otherwise $`y_{i}=0`$

6:   $`h_{i}\leftarrow\textsc{SummarizeTrajectory}(\tau_{i})`$

7: end for

8: for $`y\in\{0,1\}`$ do

9:   $`B_{y}\leftarrow\{i:y_{i}=y\}`$ $`\triangleright`$ Bucket
trajectories by verifier outcome

10:   if $`a_{y}=0`$ or $`|B_{y}|<2`$ then

11:    $`r_{i}\leftarrow 0`$ for all $`i\in B_{y}`$

12:    continue

13:   end if

14:
  $`\mathcal{C}_{y}\leftarrow\textsc{PairwiseCompare}(x,p^{\star},\{h_{i}:i\in B_{y}\},B_{y},y)`$
$`\triangleright`$ See
Algorithm [3](#alg3 "Algorithm 3 ‣ A.1 Pairwise Comparison Scheduling. ‣ Appendix A Additional Method Details ‣ Beyond Binary Verifiable Rewards: Behavioral Self-Rewarding for SWE Agents")

15:
  $`\{r_{i}:i\in B_{y}\}\leftarrow\textsc{PairwiseRewardMap}(\mathcal{C}_{y},B_{y},a_{y},\delta_{y},\tau_{y})`$
$`\triangleright`$ See
Algorithm [2](#alg2 "Algorithm 2 ‣ 3.2 From Pairwise Comparisons to Rewards ‣ 3 Method ‣ Beyond Binary Verifiable Rewards: Behavioral Self-Rewarding for SWE Agents")

16: end for

17: for $`i=1,\ldots,K`$ do

18:   $`R_{i}\leftarrow y_{i}+r_{i}`$ $`\triangleright`$ Add bounded
self-reward to verifier reward

19: end for

20: return refined rewards $`\{R_{i}\}_{i=1}^{K}`$

Algorithm 1 Behavioral Self-Rewarding with Pairwise Ranking

Outcome-separated rewarding. The judging criterion depends on the shared
verifier outcome. Among failed trajectories, the policy is asked to
identify which attempt shows more useful progress toward eventual
success. Relevant evidence includes whether the agent searched the
appropriate part of the repository, gathered useful evidence, made
directionally plausible edits, and failed in a recoverable way. Among
successful trajectories, the policy instead compares how the task was
solved: whether the agent acted efficiently, produced a targeted fix,
avoided brittle or unnecessary changes, and verified the result.
Separate rubrics distinguish progress among unsuccessful attempts from
the quality of successful execution, rather than applying the same
criterion to both outcomes.

Trajectory summarization. Raw interaction trajectories can exceed the
judge’s context length. We construct compact representations by removing
the thinking section from each step, retaining exact actions, and
truncating observations beyond a token threshold. This presents the
judge with the observable actions and their outcomes. We also include
deterministic trajectory statistics, such as command executions before
and after the final edit, as supporting evidence for the comparison. The
full representation and summarization procedure are provided in
Appendix [A.3](#A1.SS3 "A.3 Trajectory Summarization ‣ Appendix A Additional Method Details ‣ Beyond Binary Verifiable Rewards: Behavioral Self-Rewarding for SWE Agents").

Weighted pairwise comparisons. For each scheduled pair $`(i,j)`$ within
a bucket, the current policy returns a preferred trajectory
$`w_{ij}\in\{i,j\}`$ and a coarse preference-strength label
$`\alpha_{ij}\in\{1,2,3\}`$, indicating slight, clear, or strong
preference. The strength label serves as a weight when fitting the
task-local scores, retaining coarse information about the relative
preference without requiring fine-grained scalar quality judgments. To
reduce positional artifacts, we randomize the order in which the two
trajectories are presented.

### 3.2 From Pairwise Comparisons to Rewards

For each outcome bucket $`B_{y}`$, let $`\mathcal{C}_{y}`$ denote the
scheduled pairwise comparisons, each represented by
$`(i,j,w_{ij},\alpha_{ij})`$. We aggregate these weighted preferences
into task-local scores $`s_{i}`$ using a regularized weighted
Bradley–Terry model ([Bradley and Terry, 1952](#bib.bib26)), described
in
Appendix [A.2](#A1.SS2 "A.2 Weighted Bradley–Terry Score Fitting ‣ Appendix A Additional Method Details ‣ Beyond Binary Verifiable Rewards: Behavioral Self-Rewarding for SWE Agents").
These scores summarize the policy’s comparative judgments within the
bucket. To use them as auxiliary rewards, we normalize the scores, apply
a soft deadzone, and center and bound the resulting values.

Task-local score normalization. The fitted scores describe relative
preferences within a task and outcome bucket rather than a shared
quality scale across tasks. For buckets with at least two trajectories,
we standardize the scores as

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
z_{i}=\frac{s_{i}-\mu_{y}}{\sigma_{y}+\epsilon},\qquad\mu_{y}=\frac{1}{|B_{y}|}\sum_{j\in B_{y}}s_{j},\qquad\sigma_{y}^{2}=\frac{1}{|B_{y}|-1}\sum_{j\in B_{y}}(s_{j}-\mu_{y})^{2},
``` |  | (8) |

where $`\epsilon>0`$ is a small constant for numerical stability.
Buckets with fewer than two trajectories receive zero auxiliary reward
because no pairwise comparison is possible. This normalization makes the
subsequent reward map depend on relative position within the current
bucket rather than the raw scale of the fitted scores.

Soft deadzone. We apply a soft deadzone to suppress normalized scores
near zero and smoothly transform larger deviations from the bucket mean:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
u_{i}=\operatorname{sign}(z_{i})\tanh\!\left(\frac{\max(|z_{i}|-\delta_{y},0)}{\tau_{y}}\right).
``` |  | (9) |

The threshold $`\delta_{y}`$ determines the region around zero in which
scores are suppressed, following the use of thresholding to remove small
deviations ([Drucker et al., 1996](#bib.bib14); [Donoho,
1995](#bib.bib15)). Trajectories with $`|z_{i}|\leq\delta_{y}`$ have
$`u_{i}=0`$. Outside this region, the softness parameter $`\tau_{y}`$
controls how quickly $`|u_{i}|`$ approaches one.

Centering and bounding. Let

|     |                                                   |     |      |
|-----|---------------------------------------------------|-----|------|
|     |
       ``` math
       \mathcal{A}_{y}=\{i\in B_{y}:|z_{i}|>\delta_{y}\}
       ```                                                |     | (10) |

denote the active set of trajectories outside the deadzone. If
$`\mathcal{A}_{y}`$ is empty, we set $`q_{i}=0`$ for every trajectory in
the bucket. Otherwise, we center the active scores:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\bar{u}_{y}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{A}_{y}|}\sum_{j\in\mathcal{A}_{y}}u_{j},\qquad\tilde{u}_{i}=u_{i}-\bar{u}_{y},\quad i\in\mathcal{A}_{y},
``` |  | (11) |

and rescale them by their maximum absolute value within the active set:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
q_{i}=\frac{\tilde{u}_{i}}{\max_{j\in\mathcal{A}_{y}}|\tilde{u}_{j}|+\epsilon},\quad i\in\mathcal{A}_{y}.
``` |  | (12) |

For inactive trajectories $`i\notin\mathcal{A}_{y}`$, we set
$`q_{i}=0`$. The resulting scores satisfy $`q_{i}\in[-1,1]`$. Centering
makes the auxiliary signal contrastive within the active subset, while
the rescaling bounds its magnitude before applying the outcome-specific
reward amplitude.

Final reward. For trajectory $`i\in B_{y}`$, the auxiliary self-judgment
reward is

|     |                   |     |      |
|-----|-------------------|-----|------|
|     |
       ``` math
       r_{i}=a_{y}q_{i},
       ```                |     | (13) |

where $`a_{y}\geq 0`$ controls the amplitude for outcome bucket $`y`$.
Adding this refinement to the verifier reward gives

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
R_{i}=R_{\mathrm{ver}}(\tau_{i})+r_{i}=\begin{cases}1+a_{1}q_{i},&R_{\mathrm{ver}}(\tau_{i})=1,\\
a_{0}q_{i},&R_{\mathrm{ver}}(\tau_{i})=0.\end{cases}
``` |  | (14) |

Since $`q_{i}\in[-1,1]`$, passing trajectories receive rewards of at
least $`1-a_{1}`$, whereas failing trajectories receive rewards of at
most $`a_{0}`$. We choose nonnegative amplitudes satisfying

|     |                |     |      |
|-----|----------------|-----|------|
|     |
       ``` math
       a_{0}+a_{1}<1,
       ```             |     | (15) |

which guarantees that every verifier-passing trajectory receives a
higher reward than every verifier-failing trajectory. The refined
rewards are then used in group-relative policy optimization. In all-fail
rollout groups, nonconstant auxiliary rewards can restore group-relative
learning signal; in mixed-outcome groups, they provide additional
distinctions within each refined outcome bucket.

1: Comparisons $`\mathcal{C}_{y}`$, bucket $`B_{y}`$, amplitude
$`a_{y}`$, deadzone $`\delta_{y}`$, softness $`\tau_{y}`$

2:
$`\{s_{i}:i\in B_{y}\}\leftarrow\textsc{WeightedBTLFit}(\mathcal{C}_{y},B_{y})`$
$`\triangleright`$ Aggregate pairwise judgments

3: Compute $`\{z_{i}:i\in B_{y}\}`$ using
Equation [8](#S3.E8 "In 3.2 From Pairwise Comparisons to Rewards ‣ 3 Method ‣ Beyond Binary Verifiable Rewards: Behavioral Self-Rewarding for SWE Agents")
$`\triangleright`$ Normalize within the bucket

4: for $`i\in B_{y}`$ do

5:
  $`u_{i}\leftarrow\operatorname{sign}(z_{i})\tanh\!\left(\max(|z_{i}|-\delta_{y},0)/\tau_{y}\right)`$
$`\triangleright`$ Apply deadzone and soft mapping

6: end for

7: $`\mathcal{A}_{y}\leftarrow\{i\in B_{y}:|z_{i}|>\delta_{y}\}`$
$`\triangleright`$ Select trajectories outside the deadzone

8: if $`\mathcal{A}_{y}=\emptyset`$ then

9:   return $`r_{i}=0`$ for all $`i\in B_{y}`$ $`\triangleright`$ No
scores outside the deadzone

10: end if

11: Center active scores using
Equation [11](#S3.E11 "In 3.2 From Pairwise Comparisons to Rewards ‣ 3 Method ‣ Beyond Binary Verifiable Rewards: Behavioral Self-Rewarding for SWE Agents")
$`\triangleright`$ Make the signal contrastive

12: Normalize active scores using
Equation [12](#S3.E12 "In 3.2 From Pairwise Comparisons to Rewards ‣ 3 Method ‣ Beyond Binary Verifiable Rewards: Behavioral Self-Rewarding for SWE Agents")
$`\triangleright`$ Bound $`q_{i}`$ to $`[-1,1]`$

13: return $`r_{i}=a_{y}q_{i}`$ for all $`i\in B_{y}`$
$`\triangleright`$ Inactive trajectories have $`q_{i}=0`$

## 4 Experiments

#### Setup.

We use RLLM ([Tan et al., 2025](#bib.bib11)) to train on a filtered
version of R2E-Gym ([Jain et al., 2025](#bib.bib33)) and evaluate on
SWE-bench Verified ([Jimenez et al., 2024](#bib.bib22)) and
SWE-bench-Live Lite ([Zhang et al., 2026](#bib.bib18)). Training
rollouts use a maximum of 40 agent steps; evaluation uses 50 steps,
temperature 1, and three evaluation runs per checkpoint. We report
average accuracy across these runs and Pass@3, the fraction of tasks
solved by at least one of the three sampled trajectories. In the main
BSR setting, we refine only the failure bucket, with $`a_{0}=0.15`$,
$`a_{1}=0`$, $`\delta_{0}=0.5`$, and $`\tau_{0}=0.5`$. This
configuration performs similarly to or better than refining both outcome
buckets while requiring fewer pairwise comparisons
(Section [4.3](#S4.SS3 "4.3 Ablation: Verifier-Outcome Buckets ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Beyond Binary Verifiable Rewards: Behavioral Self-Rewarding for SWE Agents")).
The subsequent ablations and trajectory-behavior analysis use SWE-bench
Verified. Complete training settings are provided in
Appendix [B.1](#A2.SS1 "B.1 Detailed Setup ‣ Appendix B Additional Experiment Details, Results, and Analysis ‣ Beyond Binary Verifiable Rewards: Behavioral Self-Rewarding for SWE Agents").

### 4.1 Main Results

Table [1](#S4.T1 "Table 1 ‣ Setup. ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Beyond Binary Verifiable Rewards: Behavioral Self-Rewarding for SWE Agents")
compares BSR with verifier-only RL across two model sizes, predefined
training-step budgets, and two SWE benchmarks. BSR improves both average
accuracy and Pass@3 in every evaluated setting on SWE-bench Verified and
SWE-bench-Live. For example, on SWE-bench Verified, Qwen3-14B improves
from 32.1% to 34.7% average accuracy under the 400-step budget. On
SWE-bench-Live, the same setting improves average accuracy from 6.33% to
8.11%. The gains hold across Qwen3-14B and Qwen3-32B and across both
training budgets, indicating that the improvement is not specific to a
single model scale or training duration.
Figure [2](#S4.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 4.1 Main Results ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Beyond Binary Verifiable Rewards: Behavioral Self-Rewarding for SWE Agents")
shows the corresponding SWE-bench Verified learning curves. We
additionally evaluate on Terminal-Bench 2.1 ([Merrill et al.,
2026](#bib.bib1)). BSR improves average accuracy across all three
evaluated model and training-budget settings, full results are provided
in
Appendix [B.2](#A2.SS2 "B.2 Additional Evaluation on Terminal-Bench 2.1 ‣ Appendix B Additional Experiment Details, Results, and Analysis ‣ Beyond Binary Verifiable Rewards: Behavioral Self-Rewarding for SWE Agents").

#### Behavioral changes.

Table [2](#S4.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 4.1 Main Results ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Beyond Binary Verifiable Rewards: Behavioral Self-Rewarding for SWE Agents")
compares investigation, editing, and verification behavior. BSR more
often views a related file to the issue before the first edit (0.748
versus 0.733), achieves higher search-to-edit conversion (0.494 versus
0.465), and performs more post-edit testing (0.311 versus 0.301). These
changes coincide with fewer searches and recorded errors, alongside a
higher average number of tests. Overall, the aggregate pattern is
consistent with stronger reference-oriented investigation, search
follow-through, and verification. Full trajectory statistics and metric
definitions are provided in
Appendix [B.4](#A2.SS4 "B.4 Trajectory Behavior Statistics ‣ Appendix B Additional Experiment Details, Results, and Analysis ‣ Beyond Binary Verifiable Rewards: Behavioral Self-Rewarding for SWE Agents").

### 4.2 Ablation: Deadzone and Softness

We examine how the deadzone and softness affect the conversion of
pairwise rankings into auxiliary rewards. The deadzone suppresses
near-zero normalized scores before centering, while softness controls
how deviations outside the deadzone are transformed.
Table [3](#S4.T3 "Table 3 ‣ Behavioral changes. ‣ 4.1 Main Results ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Beyond Binary Verifiable Rewards: Behavioral Self-Rewarding for SWE Agents")
compares the full mapping with variants that remove both components or
retain the deadzone without softness. Removing both yields 32.0% average
accuracy and 45.6% Pass@3. Adding the deadzone alone raises average
accuracy to 32.6%, but lowers Pass@3 to 44.0%. The full BSR mapping
achieves 33.2% average accuracy, improving both metrics over either
simplified variant. Thus, the deadzone alone does not improve every
metric, whereas combining it with softness gives the strongest results
among the tested mappings. Full training curves are provided in
Figure [7](#A2.F7 "Figure 7 ‣ Training-time overhead. ‣ B.1 Detailed Setup ‣ Appendix B Additional Experiment Details, Results, and Analysis ‣ Beyond Binary Verifiable Rewards: Behavioral Self-Rewarding for SWE Agents")
in appendix.

| Refined bucket(s)      | Avg. | Pass@3 |
|------------------------|------|--------|
| Baseline               | 31.0 | 45.0   |
| Pass bucket only       | 32.0 | 44.0   |
| Pass + fail buckets    | 33.1 | 44.6   |
| Fail bucket only (BSR) | 33.2 | 46.6   |



Table 4: Ablation of the verifier-outcome buckets receiving BSR (%).

| Method        | Avg. acc. | Pass@3 |
|---------------|-----------|--------|
| Baseline      | 31.0      | 45.0   |

| BSR (Ours)    | 33.2      | 46.6   |



Table 5: Random-reward ablation on Qwen3-14B. Random rewards use the
same amplitude range as BSR but ignore behavioral rankings.

### 4.3 Ablation: Verifier-Outcome Buckets

We compare applying BSR to the failure bucket, the success bucket, or
both. The failure bucket includes failed trajectories from both all-fail
and mixed-outcome rollout groups.
Table [4](#S4.T4 "Table 4 ‣ 4.2 Ablation: Deadzone and Softness ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Beyond Binary Verifiable Rewards: Behavioral Self-Rewarding for SWE Agents")
shows that failure-only refinement achieves the highest average accuracy
and Pass@3, at 33.2% and 46.6%, respectively. Refining both buckets
achieves similar average accuracy of 33.1%, but lower Pass@3 of 44.6%,
while requiring additional comparisons among successful trajectories.
Success-only refinement reaches 32.0% average accuracy and 44.0% Pass@3:
it improves average accuracy over the verifier-only baseline, but does
not improve coverage across three sampled solutions. These results favor
failure-only refinement in this setting. Extending refinement to
successful trajectories increases judgment workload without improving
either reported metric over failure-only refinement. Full training
curves appear in
Figure [6](#A2.F6 "Figure 6 ‣ Training-time overhead. ‣ B.1 Detailed Setup ‣ Appendix B Additional Experiment Details, Results, and Analysis ‣ Beyond Binary Verifiable Rewards: Behavioral Self-Rewarding for SWE Agents")
in the appendix.

### 4.4 Additional Study: Random-reward control

We test whether arbitrary auxiliary rewards can reproduce BSR’s gains
without behavioral rankings. The control assigns random rewards within
the same amplitude range as BSR, but does not associate them with
pairwise trajectory preferences.
Table [5](#S4.T5 "Table 5 ‣ 4.2 Ablation: Deadzone and Softness ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Beyond Binary Verifiable Rewards: Behavioral Self-Rewarding for SWE Agents")
shows that the control achieves 30.9% average accuracy and 42.8% Pass@3,
compared with 31.0% and 45.0% for verifier-only RL. BSR instead reaches
33.2% average accuracy and 46.6% Pass@3. Random rewards therefore fail
to improve average accuracy and reduce Pass@3, whereas BSR improves
both. This shows that matching the reward amplitude alone is
insufficient to reproduce the gains from BSR’s ranking-based refinement.

## 5 Related Work

Verifiable rewards for agentic RL. RLVR uses automatic correctness
checks, with DeepSeek-R1 demonstrating its effectiveness at scale ([Guo
et al., 2025](#bib.bib17)). Building on PPO ([Schulman et al.,
2017](#bib.bib37)), GRPO removes the learned critic and normalizes
within-group rewards, GSPO uses sequence-level optimization, and LOOP
applies a leave-one-out baseline to long-horizon interactive
agents ([Shao et al., 2024](#bib.bib16); [Zheng et al.,
2025](#bib.bib7); [Chen et al., 2025a](#bib.bib34)). Hybrid-reward
methods study how additional evaluative signals can complement binary
verification. HERO combines verifier outcomes with reward-model scores
through outcome-conditioned normalization ([Tao et al.,
2026](#bib.bib4)), while PAPO integrates rubric-based process feedback
through decoupled advantage normalization ([Tan et al.,
2026](#bib.bib5)). BSR focuses on how the additional signal is obtained:
we reuse the current policy to produce task-local trajectory
preferences, then incorporate these preferences into its own training
through bounded reward refinement.

Software engineering agents, environments, and training. SWE-bench and
SWE-bench-Live benchmark real-world issue resolution ([Jimenez et al.,
2024](#bib.bib22); [Zhang et al., 2026](#bib.bib18)). SWE-agent,
Agentless, and related work explore systems and workflows for
repository-level issue resolution ([Yang et al., 2024](#bib.bib20);
[Zhang et al., 2024](#bib.bib30); [Xia et al., 2024](#bib.bib31); [Wang
et al., 2025a](#bib.bib35); [Bairi et al., 2024](#bib.bib8); [Chen et
al., 2025b](#bib.bib9)). SWE-Gym and R2E-Gym provide executable
repository-level training environments ([Pan et al., 2024](#bib.bib32);
[Jain et al., 2025](#bib.bib33)). Training approaches include SWE-RL on
software evolution data ([Wei et al., 2026](#bib.bib19)), multi-turn RL
in stateful repositories ([Golubev et al., 2025](#bib.bib36)), self-play
bug injection and repair ([Wei et al., 2025](#bib.bib12)), and CWM’s
combination of interaction traces and multi-task RL ([Copet et al.,
2025](#bib.bib10)). Methods like SWE-RM ([Shum et al.,
2026](#bib.bib13)) and SWE-TRACE ([Han et al., 2026](#bib.bib3)) develop
dedicated reward models for SWE trajectories and use them during both
training and test-time inference. BSR instead investigates whether the
acting policy itself can supply useful feedback for its own on-policy
learning. Its judgments are obtained directly from the current policy
through within-task, within-outcome comparisons, without a separate
reward-model training stage. Our experiments evaluate whether adding
this self-comparison procedure improves verifier-only training in a
fixed SWE-agent setup.

Process supervision and trajectory preferences. Process supervision
evaluates intermediate reasoning ([Lightman et al., 2024](#bib.bib25)),
while trajectory preferences support reward learning ([Christiano et
al., 2017](#bib.bib28)). Bradley–Terry aggregation and RankNet provide
pairwise-ranking foundations ([Bradley and Terry, 1952](#bib.bib26);
[Burges et al., 2005](#bib.bib27)), and DPO learns directly from
preference pairs ([Rafailov et al., 2023](#bib.bib29)). LLM-as-a-judge
methods provide model-generated evaluations ([Zheng et al.,
2023](#bib.bib23); [Liu et al., 2023](#bib.bib40)). Self-Rewarding
Language Models use the model’s own response evaluations to construct
preferences for iterative DPO ([Yuan et al., 2024](#bib.bib24)).
Process-based Self-Rewarding applies the model’s pairwise judgments to
individual mathematical reasoning steps and uses step-wise preference
optimization ([Zhang et al., 2025](#bib.bib6)). BSR builds on
self-generated feedback but studies a different judgment unit and
learning setting: observable debugging behavior across complete
tool-interaction trajectories, compared within the same task and
verifier-outcome bucket. Its preferences are aggregated into bounded
auxiliary rewards for on-policy RL, rather than used as response- or
step-level preference-optimization targets.

## 6 Conclusion

We introduced Behavioral Self-Rewarding (BSR) to investigate whether the
current policy can use its own comparative judgments to improve
software-engineering performance. BSR compares trajectories from the
same task and verifier-outcome bucket, converting task-local preferences
into bounded auxiliary rewards while preserving the verifier-defined
pass/fail ordering. By reusing the policy as a post-rollout judge, it
provides additional supervision from collected trajectories without
training a separate reward model. Experiments on SWE-bench Verified and
SWE-bench-Live Lite show improvements over verifier-only RL across the
evaluated Qwen3-14B and Qwen3-32B configurations. Together, these
results support the policy’s own comparative judgments as a complement
to binary verification, allowing distinctions among otherwise
reward-equivalent trajectories to contribute to learning from
repository-level interaction experience.

## Appendix A Additional Method Details

### A.1 Pairwise Comparison Scheduling.

Algorithm [3](#alg3 "Algorithm 3 ‣ A.1 Pairwise Comparison Scheduling. ‣ Appendix A Additional Method Details ‣ Beyond Binary Verifiable Rewards: Behavioral Self-Rewarding for SWE Agents")
describes the comparison schedule for each verifier-outcome bucket
$`B_{y}`$, where $`y\in\{0,1\}`$ denotes the shared verifier outcome.
For $`2\leq|B_{y}|<5`$, we use exhaustive pairwise comparison. For
larger buckets, we use a Swiss-style tournament schedule \[[Sauer et
al., 2021](#bib.bib21)\] to reduce the number of model calls while
maintaining balanced comparison coverage.
Table [6](#A1.T6 "Table 6 ‣ A.1 Pairwise Comparison Scheduling. ‣ Appendix A Additional Method Details ‣ Beyond Binary Verifiable Rewards: Behavioral Self-Rewarding for SWE Agents")
shows the resulting reduction in model comparisons.

For each scheduled pair, we ask the model to compare the two trajectory
summaries given the task $`x`$, reference patch $`p^{\star}`$, and
bucket outcome $`y`$. The model selects the better trajectory under the
shared outcome: better progress among failures or cleaner behavior among
successes. We denote the collection of performed comparisons by
$`\mathcal{C}_{y}`$, where each comparison record
$`(i,j,w_{ij},\alpha_{ij})`$ contains the compared pair $`(i,j)`$, the
preferred trajectory $`w_{ij}`$, and the preference-strength label
$`\alpha_{ij}`$. To reduce position bias during BSR training, we
randomize the presentation order of each pairwise comparison.

We use separate prompts for the pass and fail buckets
(Figures [9](#A2.F9 "Figure 9 ‣ B.5 Judge Quality Investigation ‣ Appendix B Additional Experiment Details, Results, and Analysis ‣ Beyond Binary Verifiable Rewards: Behavioral Self-Rewarding for SWE Agents")
and [10](#A2.F10 "Figure 10 ‣ B.5 Judge Quality Investigation ‣ Appendix B Additional Experiment Details, Results, and Analysis ‣ Beyond Binary Verifiable Rewards: Behavioral Self-Rewarding for SWE Agents")).
They have the same general structure but direct the model to different
behavioral criteria depending on the verifier outcome. We show the user
prompt in
Figure [11](#A2.F11 "Figure 11 ‣ B.5 Judge Quality Investigation ‣ Appendix B Additional Experiment Details, Results, and Analysis ‣ Beyond Binary Verifiable Rewards: Behavioral Self-Rewarding for SWE Agents")
and an example ranking response in
Figure [12](#A2.F12 "Figure 12 ‣ B.5 Judge Quality Investigation ‣ Appendix B Additional Experiment Details, Results, and Analysis ‣ Beyond Binary Verifiable Rewards: Behavioral Self-Rewarding for SWE Agents").

1: Task $`x`$, reference patch $`p^{\star}`$, model $`\pi_{\theta}`$,
trajectory summaries $`\{h_{i}:i\in B_{y}\}`$, bucket $`B_{y}`$, outcome
$`y\in\{0,1\}`$

3: $`\mathcal{C}_{y}\leftarrow\emptyset`$

4: if $`n<2`$ then

comparison is possible

6: else if $`n<5`$ then $`\triangleright`$ Case 1: Exhaustive comparison

7:   $`\mathcal{P}\leftarrow\{(i,j):i,j\in B_{y},\ i<j\}`$

   $`(w_{ij},\alpha_{ij})\leftarrow\textsc{ModelCompare}_{\pi_{\theta}}(x,p^{\star},h_{i},h_{j},y)`$

11:   end for

12: else$`\triangleright`$ Case 2: Swiss-style comparison

### A.2 Weighted Bradley–Terry Score Fitting

#### Weighted Bradley–Terry aggregation.

Given the performed comparisons $`\mathcal{C}_{y}`$ for an outcome
bucket $`B_{y}`$, we convert pairwise preferences into task-local scalar
scores using a weighted Bradley–Terry model \[[Bradley and Terry,
1952](#bib.bib26)\]. Each trajectory $`i\in B_{y}`$ is assigned a latent
score $`s_{i}`$. For a comparison between trajectories $`i`$ and $`j`$,
the model defines

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
P(i\succ j)=\sigma(s_{i}-s_{j}),\qquad\sigma(t)=\frac{1}{1+\exp(-t)}.
``` |  | (16) |

Let $`m_{ij}=1`$ if $`w_{ij}=i`$ and $`m_{ij}=0`$ otherwise. We fit the
scores by minimizing the weighted negative log likelihood with
$`\ell_{2}`$ regularization:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{BTL}}(s)=-\sum_{(i,j,w_{ij},\alpha_{ij})\in\mathcal{C}_{y}}\alpha_{ij}\left[m_{ij}\log\sigma(s_{i}-s_{j})+(1-m_{ij})\log\sigma(s_{j}-s_{i})\right]+\frac{\lambda}{2}\sum_{i\in B_{y}}s_{i}^{2}.
``` |  | (17) |

Algorithm [4](#alg4 "Algorithm 4 ‣ Weighted Bradley–Terry aggregation. ‣ A.2 Weighted Bradley–Terry Score Fitting ‣ Appendix A Additional Method Details ‣ Beyond Binary Verifiable Rewards: Behavioral Self-Rewarding for SWE Agents")
gives the optimization procedure used to obtain the scores. We use a
diagonal second-order preconditioner and re-center the scores after each
iteration, since the downstream reward map depends only on their
relative values.

1: Bucket $`B_{y}`$, comparisons $`\mathcal{C}_{y}`$, regularization
$`\lambda`$, learning rate $`\eta`$

2: Initialize $`s_{i}\leftarrow 0`$ for all $`i\in B_{y}`$

3: repeat

4:   for $`i\in B_{y}`$ do

5:    $`g_{i}\leftarrow\lambda s_{i}`$

6:    $`d_{i}\leftarrow\lambda`$

7:   end for

8:   for $`(i,j,w_{ij},\alpha_{ij})\in\mathcal{C}_{y}`$ do

9:    $`m_{ij}\leftarrow\mathbf{1}\{w_{ij}=i\}`$

10:    $`p_{ij}\leftarrow\sigma(s_{i}-s_{j})`$

11:    $`g_{i}\leftarrow g_{i}+\alpha_{ij}(p_{ij}-m_{ij})`$

12:    $`g_{j}\leftarrow g_{j}-\alpha_{ij}(p_{ij}-m_{ij})`$

13:    $`d_{i}\leftarrow d_{i}+\alpha_{ij}p_{ij}(1-p_{ij})`$

14:    $`d_{j}\leftarrow d_{j}+\alpha_{ij}p_{ij}(1-p_{ij})`$

15:   end for

16:   for $`i\in B_{y}`$ do

17:    $`s_{i}\leftarrow s_{i}-\eta\,g_{i}/(d_{i}+\epsilon)`$

18:   end for

19:   Center scores:
$`s_{i}\leftarrow s_{i}-\frac{1}{|B_{y}|}\sum_{j\in B_{y}}s_{j}`$

20: until convergence

21: return scores $`\{s_{i}:i\in B_{y}\}`$

Algorithm 4 Weighted BTL Score Fitting

### A.3 Trajectory Summarization

Before pairwise judgment, we convert each raw agent trajectory into a
compact step-wise representation $`h_{i}`$. We parse the interaction
transcript into an ordered sequence of tool actions and resulting
observations. Because the judge is intended to compare externally
visible debugging behavior, we remove the model’s internal thinking and
retain the action-observation trace. We use deterministic reductions
whenever possible and only fall back to LLM-based summarization when an
observation remains too long to preserve directly.

#### Action reparsing.

Tool actions are originally emitted in a verbose function-call format.
We parse each assistant message to extract the tool name and its
parameters, and render the action as a compact function-style call, such
as tool_name(arg=value). This preserves the invoked tool and argument
values while removing formatting overhead such as XML-style wrappers.
Multiline values are kept as multiline strings, structured values such
as lists or dictionaries are preserved, numbers and booleans are left
unquoted, and ordinary strings are JSON-escaped. If no valid tool call
is found, we retain the original action text; if a tool is found but has
no parameters, we render it as a zero-argument call.

#### Observation reduction.

Observations are reduced using tool-specific deterministic rules before
any LLM-based summarization. Short observations are kept unchanged. For
bash outputs, observations containing errors, tracebacks, or exceptions
are preserved so that failure information remains visible to the judge.
For file-editor observations, we distinguish file views from other
editor operations. When a long file view is produced by a numbered
cat-style output, we retain the first and last portions and insert a
marker indicating that the middle was omitted. Other compact file-editor
outputs are kept unchanged. If an observation remains long and does not
match one of these safe reduction cases, we summarize it with an
observation-specific prompt that preserves the key command outcome,
relevant files or paths, and any errors.

### A.4 Other Potential Instantiations of Behavioral Reward

Beyond pairwise ranking, we explored two alternative instantiations of
behavioral reward: group ranking and rubric grading. In preliminary
experiments, neither produced a clear improvement, so we did not tune or
investigate them further. Nevertheless, they illustrate other ways in
which behavioral judgment could be used to refine verifier rewards.

#### Group ranking.

Group ranking evaluates all trajectories in the same verifier-outcome
bucket jointly. Each trajectory is first summarized through a structured
process evaluation covering aspects such as localization, root-cause
analysis, fix quality, verification, and overall behavior. The judge
then considers the full group and assigns each trajectory a coarse score
from 1 to 5, with ties allowed. These scores are mapped to bounded
auxiliary rewards within the corresponding verifier-outcome bucket.
Compared with pairwise ranking, this approach gives the judge a global
view of the group and can reduce the number of direct comparison calls.

#### Rubric grading.

Rubric grading evaluates each trajectory independently against a
predefined set of behavioral criteria. The judge determines whether each
progress criterion is satisfied and whether any undesirable behavior,
represented as a red flag, is present. Unsatisfied progress criteria and
triggered red flags produce weighted penalties that refine the verifier
reward. This approach is simple, parallelizable, and provides an
absolute behavioral assessment without requiring comparisons among
trajectories.

#### Discussion.

The three approaches make different trade-offs. Pairwise ranking
provides direct relative supervision and requires only local
comparisons, but requires additional judgment compute to evaluate
multiple pairs. Group ranking compares the entire bucket more
efficiently and captures global relative structure, but its scores
remain relative to the particular group and may be sensitive to group
composition or listwise presentation. Rubric grading is less expensive
and produces an absolute assessment for each trajectory, but it does not
directly compare trajectories and depends on the completeness and
calibration of the predefined rubric. Conversely, both pairwise and
group ranking lack a task-independent absolute quality scale. Combining
absolute rubric-based assessment with comparative ranking may therefore
be a useful direction for future work.

## Appendix B Additional Experiment Details, Results, and Analysis

### B.1 Detailed Setup

We follow RLLM for training and use the filtered R2E-Gym dataset (4,578
tasks) as our training set. We show important parameters in
Table [7](#A1.T7 "Table 7 ‣ Discussion. ‣ A.4 Other Potential Instantiations of Behavioral Reward ‣ Appendix A Additional Method Details ‣ Beyond Binary Verifiable Rewards: Behavioral Self-Rewarding for SWE Agents").
We evaluate on SWE-bench Verified (500 tasks) and SWE-bench-Live Lite
(300 tasks). SWE-bench Verified is evaluated periodically throughout
training. For both benchmarks, evaluation uses a maximum of 50 agent
steps, temperature 1, and three runs. For each benchmark, we report the
mean and standard deviation of accuracy across three evaluation runs.
Pass@3 is the fraction of tasks solved in at least one of the three
runs.

For Qwen3-14B, we train on 8 GPU nodes, each containing 8 A100-SXM4-40G
GPUs. For Qwen3-32B, we use 16 nodes. Each training run takes 6 to 8
days.

#### Training observations.

For Qwen3-14B, step-limit terminations become more frequent during
training, while the truncation rate initially decreases and later rises.
The logged entropy loss also increases. We observe that more than 95% of
successful trajectories finish in fewer than 40 steps, motivating a
reduction of the training rollout limit from 50 to 40 steps. In our
experiments, this change improves performance and reduces training time,
whereas lowering the sampling temperature or adding KL regularization
reduces performance. Evaluation retains a maximum of 50 steps.

#### Kubernetes setting.

Environment provisioning is a major systems challenge for SWE-agent
training, since each optimization step may require 512 concurrent
environments ($`64`$ tasks $`\times`$ $`8`$ rollouts). In our
experiments, we manually configured a two-node Kubernetes cluster, with
each node providing 128 CPU cores and approximately 500 GB of memory. To
reduce startup latency, we pre-pull and cache all required container
images. We also use small per-pod resource requests (80 m CPU and
300 MiB memory), allowing the cluster to schedule a large number of
concurrent environments. Several configuration details are important in
practice:

- •
  Ensure that pods have outbound network access when required by the
  task.
- •
  Increase the maximum number of pods allowed per node to support the
  desired level of parallelism.
- •
  Configure Kubernetes and containerd image-garbage-collection and
  disk-eviction policies to avoid removing frequently used cached
  images.
- •
  Maintain a stable and automatically recoverable connection between the
  GPU training machines and CPU environment nodes.
- •
  Promptly clean up completed or failed pods to prevent resource
  leakage.

Additional setup instructions and configuration examples are included in
our codebase.

#### Performance optimization.

To reduce end-to-end training time, we overlap environment provisioning
with other parts of the training pipeline. First, while the model is
being updated for the current batch, we asynchronously pre-create the
environments required by the next batch. This hides a substantial
portion of environment startup latency behind model optimization.
Second, we remove the synchronization barrier between environment
creation and trajectory generation. Rather than waiting for all
environments in a batch to become ready, each rollout begins as soon as
its own environment has been created. This allows fast-starting
environments to enter trajectory generation immediately and reduces idle
time caused by slow environment initialization or other stragglers.

#### Training-time overhead.

BSR reuses the policy-serving infrastructure for post-rollout
comparisons, without a separately deployed reward model. In the measured
Qwen3-14B configuration, BSR required 19.86% more wall-clock training
time than verifier-only RL under the same training and serving GPU
allocation. This additional judging is performed during training;
evaluation uses the acting policy without BSR judge calls. While our
method results in overhead, however our method is extremely easy to
apply without additional computation resources and setup. Also,
extending verifier-only training from 270 to 400 steps does not recover
the BSR gain: BSR at 270 steps already exceeds the 400-step baseline in
average accuracy. This suggests that the improvement is not explained
simply by additional optimization steps, although a fully
compute-matched comparison remains an interesting direction. We note
that more selective comparison scheduling, improved batching, and
greater overlap between ranking and other training stages could further
reduce the cost.

### B.2 Additional Evaluation on Terminal-Bench 2.1

We additionally evaluate BSR on Terminal-Bench 2.1. Each configuration
is evaluated on 89 tasks with three independent evaluation trials.
Table [8](#A2.T8 "Table 8 ‣ Training-time overhead. ‣ B.1 Detailed Setup ‣ Appendix B Additional Experiment Details, Results, and Analysis ‣ Beyond Binary Verifiable Rewards: Behavioral Self-Rewarding for SWE Agents")
reports average accuracy across the three trials and Pass@3, the
fraction of tasks solved by at least one trial. BSR consistently
improves both average accuracy and Pass@3 across all evaluated model
sizes and training budgets, demonstrating that the gains extend beyond
the primary evaluation setting.

### B.4 Trajectory Behavior Statistics

We analyze 1,500 evaluation trajectories per method on SWE-bench
Verified from Qwen3-14B training logs and report both workload
statistics and debugging-process metrics.

#### Metrics Used.

We report two groups of trajectory-level statistics. The first group
contains basic workload statistics, including the number of steps, first
edit step, numbers of search/read/edit/test actions, post-edit tests,
errors, unique files read and edited, runtime, and token usage. These
statistics describe how the agent spends computation, but are not always
directly comparable: for example, fewer steps may indicate efficiency or
premature stopping, while more searches may indicate either careful
investigation or unfocused exploration.

The second group contains process metrics that more directly reflect
debugging behavior. *Reference file viewed before first edit* measures
whether the agent localized a reference-relevant file before editing.
*Search-to-edit conversion* measures whether search results led to
downstream edits. *Post-edit test rate* measures whether the agent
verified its changes after editing. *Duplicate command rate* captures
repeated commands. We treat these process metrics as the primary
behavioral indicators, while workload statistics provide supporting
context.

#### Behavioral Differences.

Table [9](#A2.T9 "Table 9 ‣ B.3 Additional Results ‣ Appendix B Additional Experiment Details, Results, and Analysis ‣ Beyond Binary Verifiable Rewards: Behavioral Self-Rewarding for SWE Agents")
shows that BSR improves several process metrics associated with
investigation and verification. Compared with the baseline, BSR more
often views a reference-relevant file before the first edit (0.748 vs.
0.733), has higher search-to-edit conversion (0.494 vs. 0.465), and
performs more post-edit testing (0.311 vs. 0.301). It also slightly
reduces duplicate commands (0.208 vs. 0.209). The workload statistics
are consistent with this shift: BSR uses fewer steps, performs fewer
searches, reads slightly more, runs more tests, encounters fewer errors,
and completes trajectories faster.

#### Summary.

BSR shows stronger reference-oriented investigation, search-to-edit
follow-through, and post-edit verification. These aggregate patterns are
consistent with changes in investigation and verification behavior, with
workload statistics providing complementary evidence about how the agent
allocates its debugging effort.

Figure 8: Agreement with Kimi-2.5 on sampled pairwise trajectory
comparisons over training, measured by macro F1. At each evaluation
point, 200 on-policy comparison pairs are sampled and re-evaluated using
Kimi-2.5 as an external reference judge.

### B.5 Judge Quality Investigation

We evaluate the policy’s pairwise judgments by measuring agreement with
Kimi K2.5 \[[Team et al., 2026](#bib.bib2)\] on 200 sampled comparisons
every 10 training steps. As shown in
Figure [8](#A2.F8 "Figure 8 ‣ Summary. ‣ B.4 Trajectory Behavior Statistics ‣ Appendix B Additional Experiment Details, Results, and Analysis ‣ Beyond Binary Verifiable Rewards: Behavioral Self-Rewarding for SWE Agents"),
the self-judge maintains meaningful agreement with the external judge
throughout training, with macro F1 generally around 0.6–0.7. Although
agreement decreases somewhat at later checkpoints, it remains
substantial and the corresponding BSR models continue to improve in
downstream performance. This suggests that the policy’s judgments remain
useful for reward refinement, while improving the stability of
self-judgment over training is an interesting direction for future work.
